questions.stem: A client receiving chemotherapy has a platelet count of 45,000/µL and no active bleeding. A nonurgent invasive bedside procedure is scheduled. Which nursing interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The count represents a hypercoagulable state, so the procedure should proceed without added bleeding precautions while therapeutic anticoagulation is considered.","B":"The client has thrombocytopenia and increased bleeding risk; the nurse should review procedure necessity and bleeding precautions rather than treat 45,000/µL as normal.","C":"A platelet count of 45,000/µL predicts spontaneous major bleeding in every client, so severe hemorrhage should be assumed even when examination is normal.","D":"The platelet count is clinically normal during chemotherapy because treatment-related thrombocytopenia does not increase bruising, mucosal bleeding, or procedural bleeding risk."}}
questions.rationale: Chemotherapy can lower platelet counts and increase bruising and bleeding risk. NCI guidance emphasizes that thrombocytopenia increases bleeding risk, but the exact clinical risk depends on the platelet count, other hemostatic factors, the planned procedure, and the patient's condition. The item avoids the inaccurate claim that 45,000/µL guarantees spontaneous major bleeding.
questions.source_name: National Cancer Institute — Bleeding and Bruising (Thrombocytopenia) and Cancer Treatment
questions.source_detail: Chemotherapy-related thrombocytopenia can increase bleeding and bruising risk; procedural decisions should account for the clinical context rather than assume a universal bleeding threshold.

questions.stem: A somnolent client who has been hypoventilating has an ABG with pH 7.30, PaCO₂ 55 mm Hg, and HCO₃⁻ 24 mEq/L. Which acid-base interpretation is most consistent with these data?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Metabolic acidosis, because the reduced pH is caused by a primary fall in bicarbonate while carbon dioxide rises only as respiratory compensation.","B":"Respiratory alkalosis, because the elevated carbon dioxide represents excessive ventilation and the normal bicarbonate confirms alkalemia.","C":"Acute respiratory acidosis, because acidemia is accompanied by a primary rise in PaCO₂ with little or no metabolic compensation yet apparent.","D":"Metabolic alkalosis, because a normal bicarbonate level in an acidemic client indicates primary bicarbonate retention from renal compensation."}}
questions.rationale: The ABG shows acidemia with an elevated PaCO₂ and a bicarbonate that has not risen substantially, supporting an acute primary respiratory acidosis from hypoventilation. The direction of PaCO₂, rather than a primary bicarbonate reduction or elevation, identifies the respiratory disturbance.
questions.source_detail: Respiratory acidosis is a primary increase in PaCO₂ from hypoventilation, producing acidemia; acute cases initially have limited renal bicarbonate compensation.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old adult without known ASCVD has an LDL-C of 165 mg/dL. Which statement best reflects the 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The value is considered optimal in young adulthood, so risk assessment and lifestyle counseling can be deferred until the client reaches age 40.","B":"The result automatically establishes familial hypercholesterolemia and requires the same treatment pathway as every adult with LDL-C at least 190 mg/dL in all cases.","C":"The value should be ignored if triglycerides are normal because the 2026 guideline no longer uses LDL-C in primary-prevention treatment decisions.","D":"LDL-C at least 160 mg/dL in young adulthood supports earlier risk discussion and consideration of lipid-lowering therapy rather than relying on one universal target."}}
questions.rationale: The 2026 ACC/AHA dyslipidemia guideline emphasizes earlier prevention and specifically identifies LDL-C ≥160 mg/dL in young adulthood as a setting in which pharmacotherapy may be considered, alongside lifestyle optimization and individualized risk assessment. It does not equate 165 mg/dL with the ≥190 mg/dL severe-hypercholesterolemia pathway in every patient.
questions.source_name: ACC/AHA — 2026 Guideline on the Management of Dyslipidemia
questions.source_detail: 2026 guideline supports early consideration of pharmacotherapy in young adults with LDL-C ≥160 mg/dL and uses individualized risk assessment rather than a single universal rule.

questions.stem: A client receiving a continuous unfractionated heparin infusion develops new bruising and an aPTT markedly above the unit's protocol target. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The result suggests excessive anticoagulant effect under an aPTT-based heparin protocol and requires prompt protocol-based dose review plus bleeding assessment.","B":"The aPTT directly measures platelet quantity and function, so an elevated result proves heparin-induced thrombocytopenia without checking an actual platelet count.","C":"The aPTT is the standard test for adjusting warfarin, so the heparin infusion should remain unchanged while the oral anticoagulant dose is reduced.","D":"Bruising is unrelated to heparin effect when aPTT is elevated because therapeutic heparin does not require coagulation or hematologic monitoring."}}
questions.rationale: Current heparin labeling directs dose adjustment according to coagulation testing and describes serial aPTT monitoring for continuous IV heparin, with periodic platelet count and hematocrit assessment. A markedly supratherapeutic aPTT plus new bruising warrants prompt bleeding assessment and protocol-based management; aPTT is not a platelet count and is not the principal warfarin monitoring test.
questions.source_name: DailyMed — Heparin Sodium Injection, Laboratory Monitoring for Efficacy and Safety
questions.source_detail: Full-dose continuous IV heparin is adjusted using coagulation tests including aPTT, with periodic platelet and hematocrit monitoring.

questions.stem: A client with asthma has a written action plan based on peak expiratory flow. Which statement shows correct understanding of home peak-flow monitoring?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"I will compare each reading with a population-predicted value because my own best measurement should not be used to guide an individualized action plan.","B":"I will compare readings with my established personal best and follow the written action-plan zones and instructions when values fall from that baseline.","C":"I need to measure peak flow only during a severe attack because routine or symptom-triggered trends cannot provide useful information about worsening control.","D":"If my peak flow falls, I will ignore symptoms and use the number alone because action plans should not incorporate clinical changes or medication instructions."}}
questions.rationale: GINA's current asthma-management framework supports individualized written action plans and use of peak expiratory flow when appropriate. Peak-flow action plans are interpreted relative to an individual's established personal best or agreed baseline, together with symptoms and plan instructions, rather than by one population value or isolated number alone.
questions.source_name: Global Initiative for Asthma — 2026 GINA Summary Guide
questions.source_detail: 2026 GINA guidance supports individualized asthma action plans and peak-flow monitoring referenced to the patient's personal best/baseline where PEF-based plans are used.
